question: You stage version A, edit the working file to version B, then make a plain commit. What is recorded?
options: Version A from the index
Version B because it is newest
Both as separate commits automatically
Neither until you sign in
why: The lab uses a plain commit of the staged selection. Later unstaged edits remain outside that snapshot.

question: What does the synthetic author name in a commit prove?
options: That a hosting account authenticated
That the commit records that metadata
That a teammate approved it
That the release was uploaded
why: Author metadata is distinct from account authentication, signatures, approval and publication.

question: Why record a full commit identifier instead of only the branch name?
options: Branches encrypt files
Commit names are release approvals
A branch can move to another commit
A branch never changes
why: The branch identifies a moving line of work. An exact revision makes the recorded observation specific.

question: Which ordinary command reviews the proposed next plain commit relative to HEAD?
options: git diff alone
A branch name without a command
Reading only the commit message
git diff --cached
why: The cached or staged diff compares the index with the current commit by default.

question: What can MM mean for a tracked path in short status?
options: The index and working tree both differ from their comparison states
The file is encrypted twice
Two remote servers approved it
No change can be committed
why: The first column describes the index relative to HEAD, and the second the working tree relative to the index.

question: The plain working diff is empty. What conclusion is still unsafe?
options: There are no differences in that comparison
There cannot be staged or untracked changes
The compared working contents match the index
Another status check may be useful
why: A single diff view is not a complete inventory of staged and untracked state.

question: What is the strongest reason this divergent merge has two parents?
options: Every commit has two parents
Two files force two parents
Each branch contains work after their shared ancestor
A remote server was contacted
why: The merge joins two distinct histories; the file count and network activity do not determine that relationship.

question: A merge completes without a textual conflict. What still needs checking?
options: Nothing, correctness is guaranteed
Only the color of the branch label
Whether Git created a hosting account
The integrated behavior and intended final contents
why: Mechanically compatible edits can still be semantically incompatible.

question: What happens in a fast-forward integration?
options: The branch can advance to an existing descendant without a new merge commit
All commits are erased
Every file gets copied into a second project
Authentication becomes unnecessary for future pushes
why: A fast-forward changes the reference because the desired history already contains the earlier tip.

question: What does the expected conflict return code mean in this lab?
options: All history was lost
The merge paused for a required resolution
The merge is already fully committed
A remote rejected your password
why: The scenario deliberately creates an incompatible edit so the unresolved path can be inspected.

question: Which sequence properly completes the fixed conflict scenario?
options: Delete only the marker symbols and assume success
Publish before inspecting the result
Choose correct final content, stage it, complete the merge and verify
Rename the branch without resolving the path
why: Content selection, staging, history recording and verification each answer a different part of the task.

question: Why is a clean final status insufficient evidence that a resolution is correct?
options: Clean status means there is no history
Git refuses every valid resolution
All tests run automatically on every commit
Incorrect content can also be fully committed
why: Git records the chosen contents; the requirement and behavioral checks determine whether those contents are appropriate.

question: After an additive revert, where is the mistaken commit?
options: Still present in the recorded history
Necessarily erased from every repository
Converted into a password
Automatically published as a release
why: The correction is a new commit; it does not remove the original commit from the ancestry.

question: The final file matches the baseline. Must the final commit identifier also match?
options: Yes, equal files force equal commits
No; the corrective commit has its own parent and metadata
Only if a remote is configured
Only when the branch name is short
why: Commit identity depends on more than one file’s contents, including the history relationship.

question: What cannot be concluded from this successful local revert?
options: The fixed file was restored
A corrective commit was created
A production database and all external side effects were rolled back
The earlier mistake remains visible
why: This repository has no production system or external effects. Source recovery does not perform those separate operations.

question: A receipt passed for revision A, but the branch now points to B. What is supported?
options: B is automatically approved
All future commits passed too
The branch name invalidates all historical evidence
The receipt is still evidence for A only
why: Evidence stays attached to the tested source. A new revision needs its own relevant checks.

question: Why reject a dirty working tree under this lab’s test-receipt contract?
options: It violates this local handoff’s clean-checkout requirement, even though the assertions read committed data
Dirty means the computer has malware
Git cannot read any modified file
The author identity is missing by definition
why: Dirty state fails a separate checkout-state gate before assertions. The fixed data checks read release.json from the recorded commit; they do not test modified working-tree files.

question: What should you verify before treating github.sha as the contributor’s exact branch tip?
options: Only the job name
The workflow event and actual checked-out revision
Only that the badge is green
Whether the commit message sounds confident
why: CI revision semantics depend on the event. The documented context is not a substitute for inspecting the run.

question: What does comparing an artifact with a trusted expected SHA-256 digest primarily check?
options: Whether the author is morally trustworthy
Whether every requirement is satisfied
Whether the observed bytes match that reference
Whether the file is encrypted
why: The digest comparison concerns byte integrity relative to the expected reference, not correctness or identity by itself.

question: Why control archive timestamps and file order?
options: They authenticate the publisher
They replace all tests
They publish a release automatically
Those packaging inputs can otherwise change the output bytes
why: A deterministic artifact recipe must control metadata and ordering as well as source-file contents.

question: A file and its checksum were both replaced by an untrusted sender. They match. What remains unproven?
options: The intended publisher and authorized build provenance
That a checksum can be computed
That the two received values are consistent
That bytes exist
why: An unauthenticated matching pair can be manufactured together. Identity and trusted provenance require additional evidence.

question: The tested revision and packaged revision differ without explanation. What should the handoff do?
options: Hide the older identifier
Stop the readiness claim and reconcile or retest the actual candidate
Reuse the green result because branch names match
Claim publication to avoid confusion
why: A delivery claim must refer to the contents actually tested and packaged; unexplained mismatches invalidate that connection.

question: Which statement fits this workshop’s completed local capstone?
options: The production service is deployed
GitHub approved all pull requests
The bounded local candidate and evidence were produced; hosted publication remains unperformed
A real publisher identity was cryptographically verified
why: The exercise is deliberately local, synthetic and temporary. Its evidence must stay within that scope.

question: Why keep a limitation in an otherwise successful handoff?
options: It turns a passing test into a failure
It makes exact revisions unnecessary
It authorizes remote distribution
It tells the next reviewer which claims the evidence does not support
why: Clear limits make the next decision safer and more efficient without erasing the successful bounded observations.
